utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, The Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Kardum, before we continue, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Margetts, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, just before I continue, just in terms of my expectation of the time that it may take to complete the examination-in-chief, there may be some matters that arise between the parties in respect of documents during the course of this morning's session; and taking into account those matters, I hope to be finished the examination-in-chief by the end of this first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kardum. I'd like to move on to another topic this morning, and that is the role of the civil protection department in the sanitization of the terrain. And you don't have your statements before you, but if they could be provided to you that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, for the parties and the Trial Chamber, I'd like to refer to the 2004 statement. That's 65 ter 5273 at paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the transcript, Mr. Margetts, if a reference would be made to P896, then people could more easily find it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's correct. It's P896.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if we could refer to paragraph 22 of your statement, please, and you refer in the second sentence there to the humane sanitization of the area that was to be undertaken by the civil protection, and it was also said that the crime technicians should attend and take photographs and number each body. I'd like to show you now some minutes of the crime police heads in Zagreb for the 6th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if you could please produce on the screen 65 ter 4551. And for the assistance of the parties, that was tab 48 in the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, first, Mr. Kardum, if you can see the screen on the right there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On your list it appears as being D234, which, again, Mr. Margetts, for those who might look at our transcript later --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- they will not be able to identify documents on the basis of their 65 ter numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. D234 is the 6th of August minutes of the crime police chiefs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You can see this document here, Mr. Kardum. It has the date "6 August 1995" at the top, and it says in the heading that these are minutes taken at the board meeting of the heads of the crime investigation department held on the 6th of August, 1995. And then you'll see the names of the persons present. We've already referred to Mr. Benko and Mr. Nadj in the course of your evidence, and there are names, also, of other department chiefs. Now if I could refer you to Item 2, that refers to the functioning of the department for war crimes and terrorism, and refers at Item B to the work of the collection centres. And then, if I could refer you to Item 3, and that's what I'd like you to pay attention to. And if you could just read through Item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, that's at the bottom of the page of the B/C/S, so if that could be highlighted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Kardum, once you've read the text there that appears under the heading AD-1, if you could indicate, and then we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we could please move to the next page, and just the portion there that sets out the assignments, and there's a reference to both Mr. Maric and Mr. Cemerin, and then a reference to Mr. Zidovec who is to liaise with the HV regarding hygiene and sanitation measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Can you please confirm that these assignments set by the chiefs of the crime police department are the forensic assignments that you were referring to in paragraph 22 of your 2004 statement.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first time that I see this text. This is a text from the ministry. I've never seen it before, and we in the police administration including that one of Zadar and Knin received a quite different document from this one. But as a rule, as far as I can see, for at least from this portion that I have managed to read, this coincides with what was done in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum, and now you just referred to a document that you would have received in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if I could please move to 65 ter 4951, and that's tab 58 for the parties on the exhibit list. And, Mr. Registrar, if you could just move to the second page in the B/C/S. Oh, thank you, Mr. Registrar, just down --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You'll see there, Mr. Kardum, that this is signed by Mr. Maric who is mentioned in the crime police department minutes for 6 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we just go up to the top of the document again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You'll see that it's dated the 6th of August, and it's addressed to the criminal police chiefs. Is this the document that you received that you were referring to in the course of your last answer?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received this document, but in a different form. Obviously your source is directly the MUP because I got it from the teleprinter and this one is type-written, as did the other chiefs of the criminal police of the other police administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this document could be given an exhibit number and entered into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since there are no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number P898.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P898 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, how many sanitation teams were there operating in the field during August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many teams there were because the sanitation of the field was not within my competence. The sanitation of the terrain was exclusively within the competence of the civilian protection, and it was supported according to this order -- or rather, according to another order, they were supported by us in terms of forensic services. As in Zadar, we did not have enough crime scene examiners. The forensic service people, they came from other police administrations. Those were Varazdin, Split and Dalmatia. I think in Knin, in the area of Knin, it was the Split-Dalmatia administration that gave them support. In the Lika area, it was from the Medjugorje or the Varazdin police administration. As I already said, I only had 12 crime scene examiners in the holding centre for POWs, and they were doing, also, their daily work so that they could only partially support the people doing the sanitation work in the field. But this was regulated by a different order, not this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Ms. Kardum, just in terms of the numbers of crime scene examiners you had, you said you had 12 crime scene examiners who were engaged in the holding centre for POWs. Did you have any additional crime scene examiners to those 12, or is that the full complement of crime scene examiners that you had?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crime scene examiners, the forensics, examiners of the crime scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, there were -- these jobs are very extensive, every on-the-site investigation requires the presence of crime scene examiners to attend the scene and to make these sketches --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, in terms of their activities, that's other issue. I'm just interested in the resources you had at your disposal, and you said that you only had 12 crime scene examiners in the holding centre for POWs, and they were also doing their daily work, and they could only partially support sanitation. My question is in addition to these 12 crime scene examiners, did you have any other crime scene examiners, or did you only have 12 at your disposal in the month of August 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, page 6, line 13 and 14 the answer is "yes." The witness verified with you whether your question was about crime scene examiners. You said yes. And then the witness answered your question that he had - at least that's how I understood your answer - that you had additional crime scene examiners. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Unfortunately, that may my question was not put in the best way. I provided an option to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then put it now in a better way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did you have any additional crime scene examiners to the 12 that you were engaged in the POW centre?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 12 crime scene examiners that I had in my police force prior to the Oluja were taken over -- they took over -- in addition to the regular duties, which they normally did, they also took over assignments in the POW holding centre and partly also supported the sanitation effort. For these jobs, civilian protection also was given people from the Split and Dalmatia people -- police administration. I don't know whether one or two. One of the men was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Sutor [phoen] by his last name and then two or three people from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kardum, I think it's abundantly clear now on the record, but just to be certain, you only had 12 crime scene examiners subordinated to you during August 1995, correct? And if you could answer yes or no, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. Now, when the crime scene examiners were engaged in their sanitation tasks, how many of them went to the scene where the bodies were found?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never was with them at such places. They only assisted the civilian protection people and did precisely those jobs which were assigned to them by telegram from the MUP, which I believe arrived on the 5th of August, 1995, and I'm sure that have you that order. I suppose that one CSE went to attend the scene, possibly two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. I'd now like to refer you to your 2007 statement, and that is now P897, and I'd like to paragraph you to paragraph 8 of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if P897 could be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, if you go to paragraph 8 of your 2007 statement, and you will recall this having reviewed it yesterday. There's a reference to the Knin police administration daily log of events, and there is a reference to 30 bodies discovered in August of 1995. And in the final sentence of paragraph 8, you confirm that there's no reference to the criminal police, and you say you do not recall being informed of any criminal investigation into any murder in Knin in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could please have displayed on the screen 65 ter 4559, which is also D235, the exhibit D235, and is located at tab 49 of the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, this is, again, minutes of the crime police chiefs. And, again, it's the -- it's the heads of the crime police in Zagreb and the minutes of their meeting. You'll see that Mr. Benko is not present but Mr. Nadj is, and you'll see that the agenda is both tasks in relation to clearing up the terrain and tasks in relation to collection centres. And I'd like to refer you to Item 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that's just under AD-1 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if you could please read through the reference there for Agenda Item 1, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see this document for the first time. I have had no occasion to see this document generated in the ministry so far, and as such it had never been sent to us. I'd just like to comment on this AD-2 part of it. Where it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'll give you an opportunity to comment in relation to Agenda Item 2. My first question is in relation to Agenda Item 1. Now, if you've had an opportunity to read that, I'd just like that ask you the question. Is the reference there to that -- to the tasks of clearing up the terrain where it states that: "Our task is to carry out the identification of persons in the prescribed manner, and it is not necessary to conduct on-site investigations." Is that consistent with the records that appear in the Knin diary and your reference to the fact that you did not investigate killings in Knin in August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not. This is not consistent with the actual state of affairs, although this order or these minutes quite clearly state their business. I will give you a few examples where we did this, investigated criminal offenses in the area of Knin: Gosic, a criminal offence of murder of seven civilians which happened on the 27th of August in 1995. We investigated that, and we apprehended the perpetrators. This process took a long time. However, that area was transferred from the Zadar-Knin PU to the Sibenik PU. So it was returned to its original area of Sibenik, to its competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kardum, if you could just at this stage --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I can document this by further examples. We investigated these offences in 2001 or 2002. We also detected the perpetrators, also, from the 5th or 6th of August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, first of all, you asked the witness whether this was consistent with his statement, and he explains to us now why it's not consistent. At the same time, we do not need details at this moment. If you say it's not consistent because we investigated a murder seven civilians committed there, then we -- at this moment we do not need how exactly the investigations went on, to whom the case file was passed, et cetera. So give the examples which demonstrate the inconsistency, but make it very brief. Please proceed. You've given us one example. There's another one. Could you very briefly describe the other example, that is date, place, kind of -- the kind of investigation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you more examples of our investigations if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kardum, if you could just specify in addition to the Gosic investigation in August of 1995, what other investigations into killings did you undertake?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragina Punos, a person killed on the 5th or 6th of August, 1995. Parts of the body were found in April 1996, and an on-the-site investigation was carried out by the investigating judge, a pathologist, and on the basis of the parts of the body found, the cause of death could not be established, but by later processing in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. You apparently are referring to an on-site investigation in April 1996. Mr. Margetts was asking you about the consistency with your statement, and your statement is about August 1995. So on-site investigations on dead bodies found in August 1995. Could you give us another example apart from the Gosic incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact date, whether it was August, the end of August, or the beginning of September. Sava Babic was a person who was killed, and we tried to find the perpetrator. Then Savo Sulaja [phoen], Manda Tisma [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could ask you -- you said you're not certain about the date of Sava Babic. Could you tell us the place? What was the place where Sava Babic was found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it was in Nevosevci [phoen] or Mokro Polje. I think in Mokro Polje in the Knin area, the general area of Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kardum, the reference in your statement as His Honour has pointed out is to the on-site investigations conducted in August 1995; and similarly, the minutes that we're referring to are directives for the conduct of the forensic examiners in -- from the date 7 August 1995. And so that's what we're interested in: The activity of on-site investigation that you conducted in that period, not in relation to crimes that may have occurred in that period but the actual activity of your forensic examiners in that period. Now, in addition to Gosic, can you tell the Court of a specific investigation conducted in August 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just mentioned them. The ones that I've already listed, they were conducted at the end of August. Some of them were also conducted in September and some even a few years later. I just want to make something clear. Item 1 is consistent with the actual situation. In other words, partly consistent, where the hygiene and sanitation of the field was carried out. A team went out and found a decomposed body. So obviously that person had died at some earlier age. We did not investigate how this person was -- how this person died but just carried out the instructions as contained in the order from August -- 1995. We were also afraid that there may be some epidemics, and we simply acted on the order. As I said, I've never received an order where it said that we should not conduct investigations. At least, I never got such an order. Maybe the civilian protection did, but I was never told not to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Furthermore -- I apologise. But when soldiers are concerned, the Croatian civilian police did not conduct investigations into Croatian soldiers, where victims or killed persons, dead persons were soldiers. We just considered this to be deaths in combat, and there was no need to conduct an investigation. Now, if there was -- if there was any illegal activity, then we would contact the military police and then perhaps engage in some joint investigation, joint queries, and so on. However, there were no such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. You said when soldiers are concerned, the Croatian civilian police did not conduct investigations into Croatian soldiers. Were you focussing just on Croatian soldiers or on whatever kind of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I wasn't clear enough. We did not conduct investigations in the cases where the victims were Croatian soldiers. Is it clearer now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I'm not talking about Croatian soldiers as perpetrators but as victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you say, We did not investigate Croatian soldiers. If the soldiers would be, for example, Serb soldiers of the ARSK, would you then investigate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we're talking about combat, a battle that was on the 5th of August, we did not investigate it regardless of who was killed, whether Serbian or Croatian soldiers. For us, these were casualties in combat and we did not consider that we needed to carry out an investigation. Had we learned that a Serbian soldier was arrested and then illegally detained or that a crime -- a war crime had been committed, then we would get involved by informing the crime service of the military police and then investigating the matter with them together because what we were concerned with was the crime itself, not the perpetrator. That was the second stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Just in relation to this issue, Mr. Kardum, you did address the issue of soldiers suspected of committing crimes in your 2004 statement, and that's at paragraph 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's P896. And paragraph 25, Mr. Registrar, if that could please be presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, if I could refer you to what you said. You said: "If a soldier was suspected of committing a crime, it was the responsibility of that soldier's command to report that fact to the military police who had their own crime police." And then you refer further on to: "The military police could ask for help from the civilian police if they needed it." And: "When a crime is reported to the civilian police, they report that crime to the military police." Now, I'd just like to refer you to a document. It's 65 ter 1735.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If that could be presented on the screen, please, Mr. Registrar, and that's at tab 63.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, you'll see that that document is dated 12 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if we could go over the page, if -- over the page to see who the author of the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now the author is Mario Tomasovic, assistant commander for political affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Registrar, if we could please return to the first page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you'll see that this is a 12 August 1995 warning to the assistant commanders for political affairs. If you just read through that document.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read the first page. Could I see the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, have you completed reading that document?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I refer back to the first page of the B/C/S, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kardum, the first part I'd like to refer you to is the start of the second paragraph, which is the sentence that appears above the bolded type. And this document refers to the irresponsibility of individual soldiers, non-commissioned officers, AND officers who compromise the Croatian army and state through their inappropriate conduct and acts. And then if we look below, enumerated at 1 to 4 are various acts and indicates that it's necessary to prevent these acts. That's "the continued torching and destruction of facilities and property; killing of livestock; confiscation of property; and inappropriate conduct toward remaining civilians and prisoners of war." My first question is this: You were on the territory at this time; did you observe these acts, these acts that are enumerated 1 to 4?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time that I see this document. It's a military document, not a document by the civilian police. There is no mention made of the civilian police anywhere, and I think it doesn't concern the civilian police. And I don't think it is an appropriate for me to comment any -- on any part of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, the question is not whether you would comment on it. The question was whether you observed things as described in this letter. That is, the continued torching and destruction; the killing of livestock; confiscation of property; and inappropriate conduct toward remaining civilians and prisoners of war. Did you observe these kind of things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were such things, and we took action against the perpetrators at this time. The killing of livestock, I'm not sure about that. I never saw that. This is the first time that I hear of it. I know that there was collection of livestock, gathering of livestock, but whether there was killing of livestock, I don't know about that. The treatment or the conduct toward members and soldiers of the peace forces, I'm not aware of that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, you indicated that, yes, you're aware of such things, and you said you took action against the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And in this document here, the referenced individuals are soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers who compromise the Croatian army. Did you, in the crime police, take action in August 1995 against individual soldiers, non-commissioned officers, and officers of the Croatian army for the perpetration of the acts listed at 1 to 4?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not take action toward officers. We didn't have any non-commissioned officers. Whether there were some soldiers, I don't know. I know that we did run into some soldiers, privates, confiscating property or taking property away, actually. But it's hard to precisely say whether someone was a soldier or not because at this time demobilisation was in process, so whether someone was a soldier at the actual moment that's -- I wasn't really aware of that. However, there were lists and registers, and your team had the opportunity to gain insight into all such registered complaints, and we were asked to submit someone hundred or so complaints. This was done through the Ministry of Justice. But whether there were some privates or not involved, I can't really tell. Mainly, the issue or the crime at stake was the taking-away of property, but I have to stress again that I'm really not sure whether at that particular point in time there were privates or not, whether there were soldiers or not, because there were a lot of people taking stuff away who were wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kardum, you've referred to the fact that we've had the opportunity to take lists and registers. So the action that you took, is that recorded in the crime registers?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. Maybe not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: In accordance with the procedures that the crime police adopted in terms of recording the action they took, in terms of the extent to which those procedures were followed, would it be the case that all of your -- all of the actions you took were in those -- were recorded in those crime registers?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The crime police department did not have crime registers. We did not maintain them. But as I've already mentioned, each criminal complaint was registered in the log-book. Before it was forwarded to the district attorney, it was entered in the crime register of the police station, of the police station on whose -- on the territory of which the crime had been committed, unless -- unless the perpetrator was a minor, in which case that complaint would have been submitted at the place where the minor lived and not where the crime was committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate to the Court specific examples of action that your crime police took during August 1995 against Croatian soldiers in relation to incidents of the burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Did your crime police take any action against any Croatian soldiers during August 1995, in relation to incidents of the burning of houses?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure at this point in time. I think we did not record such incidents. However, I do have to say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- when torching of houses was in question --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- I didn't ask you about the recording. I asked you whether you took any action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could finish his answer. You said you did not record such incidents; however, you had to say something. Would you please complete that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we had major difficulties with the torching of houses because the lay of the land was as it was. It's a hilly area, a large area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you there. You said: "I think we did not record such incidents. However ..." The question was whether you took any action. So what -- I, therefore, would like to know whether, although not recorded, you nevertheless took action in relation to torching incidents. Did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Action was taken. But as I've already said, if you were following closely, about two per cent of the entire police force was under my command. The police was focussed on covering the area with uniformed policemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as for me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking broad explanations but, rather, focus on you said: We did not record such incidents. However, we took action. Could you give one example of such action taken although not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I recall, for instance, that we processed a policeman who had torched six houses. He was a member of our police force, the regular police, and he torched six houses in a village in the Knin area with two women burning to death in those houses. We processed this incident --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- no. The question was focussing on torching committed by Croatian soldiers, not by policemen, not by civilians. Did you take any action against Croatian soldiers suspected of being involved in torching houses, August 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that there were such suspicions that Croatian soldiers torched houses. It's possible that there were such incidents, but I really can't recall now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, I'd now like to refer you to crime police chief -- the minutes of the crime police chiefs of 12 August 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's 65 ter 5024, Mr. Registrar, if you could please display that on the screen. It's tab 50 in the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, this is the 12th of August, 1995, the same date as the previous document that we saw. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous document has received no exhibit number yet or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's an omission. I would like to move that into evidence, and if I could have an exhibit number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was 65 ter 1735 or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 1735. I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number P918.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P918, and for those who are surprised by the numbering, that's, of course, caused by the meanwhile-prepared list in which provisionally exhibit numbers are assigned to documents attached to the 92 ter statements and which goes until P917. P918 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kardum, you'll see again that at this particular meeting on the 12th of August, the department chiefs were in attendance, and for a part of the time so was minister -- Assistant Minister Benko. And I'd just like to refer you to the first paragraph under Agenda Item 1. And you will see that Mr. Milinovic and Mr. Turkalj agreed following consultations with Mr. Grujic and civilian protection duty officer that the procedure in the newly established centres for reception of persons refusing to go to Serbia will be carried out the same way as in admission centres for civilian persons. And the crime police is to check the list of persons with the purpose of possible detection of wanted persons or perpetrators of crime. Now my question is, and it relates back to the issues we discussed yesterday and also provoked by these minutes: Why were the civilians in the reception centres?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, why were civilians in reception centres? This question is put to me. Perhaps my level is not high enough to answer that question. However, I will clarify it. First of all, when civilians were brought in - and I don't know under whose instructions or whose order - it wasn't from the police -- from the Zadar-Knin administration. However, the fact is that those civilians did not possess Croatian documents. They had no documents whatsoever on them. And they were brought to these holding centres or reception centres primarily so that they may be issued documents, and as I've already mentioned, most of these people were elderly, infirmed, and many of them were mentally retarded. I'm sorry I have to use that term, but that's how it was. These were persons who had been abandoned by their families who took care of them in the past and who left, leaving them behind. I think that the treatment of civilians was always guided and exclusively guided by humanitarian principles of caring for those individuals. Assuming that this question may arise here, I brought with me a document, a list of police officers, our police officers, who -- who brought with them from the Srb area 12 civilians, produce their documents at the police station in Lapac, and returned them on the same day to their homes. However, in the early days that was not possible because there was a large number of civilians, and those services were just being established. Many of these people needed medication. Many needed to be hospitalised or treated and so on and so forth. So what is at stake here is the following: They had no documents - that was a fact - their documents had to be produced for them, and most of these people were incapable of taking care of themselves. So when they arrived at the reception centres, they were not within the competence of the civilian police. They were within the competence of the organisation for refugees and the Red Cross. As for this portion of the text which says that the treatment will be same as in admission centre for civilian persons and that crime -- criminal complaints will be -- or criminal action will be taken against any who disobey this order, that is true. For instance, I can give you an example of Zoran Cvjianovic for whom it was determined that he had killed Josip Zelic, that he was perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: That's fine. I'd just like to refer you back to these minutes and the reference is to persons refusing to go to Serbia. Now, at that stage, a lot of Serb civilians, were they not refusing to go to Serbia, or in fact, were they electing to go to Serbia or to leave the territory?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, these people had a number of possibilities. One was to remain at their homes; another was for them to go to Serbia, to stay with their relatives because members of their families had already gone there, younger family members; and the third option was for them to go to third countries. It was their own choice, and they made it, but that was not a result of the work in the police administrations. As can you see, these documents were produced in the Ministry of the Interior, and the authors and participants of and participants in these documents are known persons, and none of these persons is directly subordinate to me. So perhaps it would be more proper to ask these persons for comments on such matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. When we looked at -- a moment ago, we looked at P918, and we looked at the four incidents of crime that were occurring on the territory, and you said you'd observed those -- those events. Do you think that those events had an impact on the remaining Serbs and affected their actions as to whether or not they left or remained on the territory?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. That is hard to comment on because at those moments those areas were isolated in a way. People from one village could not know what was happening in another village in order to be able to make decisions on that basis to the effect I'm going to leave this area or I'm not going to leave this area. But in principle, I know that Croatian humanitarian organisations visited those people, took relief in food and other aid to them and that the state even helped them in money. In fact, we registered in the field that our policemen looked after these people and so did Croatian soldiers. In many instances, I heard very nice words by Serbs in respect of those soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me stop you -- let me stop you there. The question was not how well people who had remained in the villages were looked after. The question was whether you think that the crimes described in the other document we just saw - that is the continued torching of houses and confiscation of property - whether that would have influenced the choice of those who were in the reception centre, the choice whether to return to their homes or to leave for Serbia. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether those people actually were aware what was happening. If they were not there, how could they know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President I'd now like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just a housekeeping matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A housekeeping matter. We're referring to P918, but I've found that that document is already in evidence as D645, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D645. That would then -- that's the letter from Mario Tomasovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although there is no date on your list, Mr. -- it was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: 12th of August, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 12 of August. Could you please verify so that -- perhaps, Mr. Registrar, you also can compare with D645, and if it's the same document, then I think P918 could be vacated and used again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And, Mr. President, if 65 ter 5024, the 12 August 1995 minutes from the meeting of the crime police chiefs could be given an exhibit number and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar, 65 ter 5024 would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That becomes Exhibit number P919, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P919 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, possibly if we've vacated P918, would it be possible for this exhibit to be given that number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's possible, this one or the other one, but since it has not been finally -- I asked you to verify -- I asked Mr. Registrar to verify and only then to vacate that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but it certainly will be used if it's available. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I'd now like to refer to a document which is D510, and it's at tab 44 or it's 44 on the exhibit list. And Mr. Registrar, if that document could please be displayed, in particular page 4 of the English and page 5 of the B/C/S. Now, there's just been a discussion between the parties and agreed amendment to the translation of this document, Your Honours, and I'd like to bring your attention to that amendment, for the reason that the document was previously introduced into evidence during the course of cross-examination of an earlier witness, Witness 86. And I'd like to just indicate to Your Honours the amendments. You'll see, if we look at Section 3, "Taking In" -- headed: "Taking In", if we look at the last line of the first paragraph, and -- or the last sentence refers to -- at the conclusion sentence: "An official shall take in a military person if this cannot be carried out by..." Now, the words "may not" have been replaced with the word "cannot." The same amendment has been made in the second line of Section 4, where it says that "MUP officials. If this cannot be carried out..." The previous words were "may not". And, Mr. Registrar, if we could go down in the English, please. Your Honours, there was a sentence that had been missed in the translation, and it's -- it commences six lines from the bottom of the page, and that sentence is: "Therefore, for a legal implementation of the means of coercion against a military person, it is essential to find out whether it was possible for the military police to have intervened in a timely manner." And I just put that on the record that this amended translation has now been uploaded, and during the course of the examination of the previous witness we didn't have the benefit of that additional sentence, and the -- the additional information that we received from the amendment of the words "may not" to "cannot" in Sections 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you can look on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I do understand there's agreement on this. Therefore, Mr. Registrar, then the D510, the translation can be replaced by the now-revised translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if you can look at Section 5 of the document that's displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, possibly if we can bring up Section 5 more to the centre of the screen in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, please indicate when you've completed reading this page and we can move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it. I don't know what it is that you want from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. And then if you can just pay attention to the remainder of Section 5 there. Please indicate when you've completed reading that.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, you will see in the section on this page here, the reference in the second-last sentence to the fact that for the -- for means of coercion to be implemented by a civilian policeman against a military person, it's essential to find out whether it was possible for the military police to have intervened in a timely manner. And you have referred to the relative authority of the civilian police and the military police over military suspects, and I'd just like to ask you: Is that consistent with your understanding? That is, if it was possible for the military police to intervene in a timely manner, then the civilian police were not able to intervene against a military perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Would you be so kind as to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kardum, in your statement you've referred to the fact that the primary responsibility in terms of the reporting of crimes and the apprehension of military suspects was the responsibility of commanders, in terms of reporting it to military police, and the military police, in terms of apprehending the military suspects and investigating the matter. So, this document here states that, in fact, if it was possible for the military police to have intervened in a timely manner, then the civilian police did not have the legal right to intervene against a military perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask that the question be put in its full context. The next sentence puts that in context and says that it's not just a question of what -- how we define -- it should be put to him. The next sentence, I think, is key.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. -- let's do it as complete as possible, not leaving out the details. Could you please rephrase your question, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You'll note, Mr. Kardum, that Mr. Misetic has indicated that the following sentence also is relevant to this question, and so look -- I'll take the words of the following sentence, and that is it concludes that the implementation of coercion by authorised officials being the civilian police would be considered illegal should it be established that the military police had been able to intervene in due time. Now, is that consistent with your understanding of the relative authority of the civilian police and the military police over suspected military perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where these instructions were generated at all. I see them for the first time, but I do know this. If a military was the perpetrator of a criminal offence, he would be handled by the military police. If that person was in civilian clothes, then the civilian police would handle up to the moment until that person is identified as a member of the military staff. At that time, the civilian police would then so inform the military police. That is the way we proceeded. And if possibly the civilian police found a military in the commission of a criminal offence, they would detain that person and inform the military police which had the obligation to take over such a person for further processing. I believe that I was clear on that. Those were the rules of behaviour, rules of conduct which we observed, but this is the first time that I see this in written form. I'm not sure whether I quite understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kardum. You did, and I thank you for the answer. I'd now like to refer you to a document which has been introduced into evidence as Exhibit D49. That's at tab 5 or number 5 in the exhibit list. It's an order of Josko Moric.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, if that could please be brought up on the screen. It's an order of Josko Moric dated 18 August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: You will have reviewed this document in the course of your reading of your materials yesterday, and it is referred to in your statement, paragraphs 9 and 10 of your 2007 statement. So I'd like to move you to straight to paragraph 5 of this order, if I may. And you'll see at paragraph 5 there's a reference to, again, a situation where the military police cannot perform a task, and that task is the task described in Item 4, that the civilian police will do it alone. Now, is that also consistent with your understanding of the distinction between the role of the civilian police and the military police, or does that in any way change the normal arrangements; that is, where the military police cannot perform the task of on-site investigations and forensic and operative criminal processing, then the civilian police will do it alone, irrespective whether the perpetrate wears a Croatian army uniform or not. So that means that there will be instances where there are suspected military perpetrators and the civilian police are conducting the on-site investigation and forensic and operative criminal processing. Is that consistent with your understanding of the -- of the relation between the military police and the civilian police, or does this order, in fact, change that in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just going to object because I think it's a very compound question, and I'm not sure I'm following what the question actually is asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're concerned whether the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Margetts, is there any possibility that you make the question less of a compound question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. And I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And I'll make it more grounded in the actual events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: After the 18th of August, 1995, did you conduct on-site investigation and forensic and operative criminal processing in cases where you suspected that the perpetrator was a military person without any assistance or -- from the military police?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you assume that we cannot know who a perpetrator of a criminal offence if we don't know who the perpetrator is. This is not the way --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- it goes. If we have a criminal offence, the way we proceed -- we actually proceed according to the criminal offence in question, and only after having investigated the criminal offence we come by information that the possible perpetrators are members of the army, we would in that -- such case certainly inform the military police, and then we would agree on our further procedure with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you -- let me stop you there because you are not focussing your answer on the question that was put to you. You have seen in paragraph 4 of this document that there should be an agreement between -- that at least the police administration chiefs, I understand the civilian police administration chiefs should meet with the commanders of the military police battalions that we found in paragraph 1. Then in paragraph 4, it says that they should agree that an on-site investigation and forensic and operative criminal processing should be conducted after every case of torching of houses and illegal taking-away of people's moveable property. Now, in paragraph 5, we find that if the military police cannot perform the task, the task I just mentioned, that the civilian police will do it alone, even if the perpetrator wears a Croatian army uniform. Now, the question was, did you ever conduct an on-site investigation and forensic and operative criminal processing just on your own, without the military police against a perpetrator wearing a Croatian army uniform, where the military police could not perform those tasks? Did this ever happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did conduct on-site investigations not knowing who the perpetrator was, and we did not conduct the processing without the knowledge of the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you said you did conduct on-site investigation no knowing who the perpetrator was. Did you ever conduct an on-site investigation in case it was reported to you or where you had reasons to believe that the perpetrator was wearing a Croatian army uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'd have to think about it to try and remember because I did not attend the on-site investigations. Yes, there were some cases of that. I just remembered. There were -- there was, for instance, the report of the criminal offence of rape in Knin and that the injured party suspected in advance, I believe, a uniformed person to have been the culprit. I will not say a soldier, but a person in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was -- that criminal offence was solved and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this document talks about the cases of torching of houses and illegal taking-away of people's moveable property. At the same time, Mr. Margetts, it seems not to be perfectly clear whether in paragraph 5 where reference that made to the tasks also would refer to the limitation of the type of crimes involved. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kardum, can you refer to any instance in August 1995 where you suspected that there was a military perpetrator and you proceeded without the involvement of the military police to investigate a crime of the torching of houses or illegal taking-away of people's moveable property?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there exists a large number of such criminal offences of the unlawful seizure of property with the perpetrators being the Croatian soldiers, and these cases haven't been processed by the Croatian police. This usually happened in this way. The Croatian police had check-points, that it had manned for a while together with the military police. I don't know exactly on what dates, but we do have the relevant records. And when people passed by those roads, it often happened that a Croatian soldier would be passing through, carting off some stolen property or property that he could not prove was his property. So we would process such a soldier, seize such property, and prosecute the person in question, file a criminal complaint, and most often in cooperation with the military police. In any case, the military police was informed of it. All such criminal complaints are documented. They are filed in our criminal registers and have been referred to the district attorneys in charge and so on and so forth. In Zadar, we had a murder case where a Croatian soldier had killed a civilian in an argument, in a brawl. I believe that the civilian was also a Croat. His name was Bencun, as -- if I remember correctly. The military police was informed, and the civilian police and military police co-operated and conducted the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kardum --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge was duly informed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You are giving us now details of where you worked together when the question was focussing on situations where the military police could not perform the task and that you did it alone. That was the question, and that is what you read in paragraph 5 of this document. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts. May I ask you really to focus your answers, listen carefully to the question, and focus your answers not on the whole of the situation but specifically on the circumstances that were mentioned in the question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I do have another topic that I'd like to move to, and I could start that now if that would be convenient, or...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, would it be your last topic or would it...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. -- well, there's this topic and then there's just one further matter, which may be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I think about 15 minutes.

utterances.text: Then I think it's better to have the break first.
