We'll have a break, and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, it's the first of your 15 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if I could please call up 65 ter 5469. Just for the party's reference, this is not on the exhibit list because this is the document that Mr. Kardum presented to us yesterday. We've had a translation of the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, may I take it that Defence has also had a opportunity to look not only at the original but also at the translation. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And so if we could move that into evidence and it could be given an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P920, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P920 is admitted into evidence, which gives me an opportunity to return to P918, where it was said that this was the same document as D645. Although the content of the document seems to be the same, the documents are not identical. Apparently, they come from a different source. Apart from some handwriting, which seems not to be very important, the stamps on the document on the second page are not put in the same position; and D645, I take it that at the back it stands for a copy or that there's a copy taken from some archives which does not appear on the other one. So, therefore, not knowing exactly what the importance of that could be under any circumstance, we leave 65 ter 1735 at this moment to be P918 and not to vacate P918.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the other document that is on our screen, the document the witness brought yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's correct. And if that P920 could be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you have not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, Your Honour. [Overlapping speakers] Correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think I said so already on page 36, line 22. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Madam Registrar, if you could please display P57 on the screen, and that's page 64 of the B/C/S and page 54 of the English, please. Yes. Madam Registrar, I apologise. It is in fact D57; that's my error. The Knin police station log-book. It's item -- Tab 4 on the exhibit list, formerly 65 ter 4473. That's D57, please. And, Madam Registrar, if you could move on the B/C/S copy to page 03622706, so that will be nine page earlier than the page that's currently displayed. And the entry in the English, Your Honours, that I'm looking at is the Entry 180 which is currently displayed in the English. And that's the one at the bottom of the screen. And correct, that's the entry we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, could you please look at Entry 180. This is the Knin police station daily log of events, and you'll see that there's a reference there. There's a report in relation to a person being killed, and the duty officer -- the operational duty service of Zadar-Knin was informed, and they referred the person making this entry to crime police chief Kardum who passed on the case to operational officers of the Knin district police administration, crime police. And then it follows. Do you recall receiving this information from the operational duty service of the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And if I could refer you to the reference there --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It's the 25th of August, 1995. Now, if I could just refer you, it says that you passed on the case to operational officers of the Knin district police administration, crime police. Who were the operational officers in Knin at that time, that is, the 25th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the dates here, mentioned here, there were no crime police in the police station Knin except those two who worked at the reception centre for civilians in Knin. But I can see here a name mentioned, "I. Petkovic." I think this should be the fourth person, Ivica Petkovic. He was a police officer of one of the police stations in Zadar. I have no idea why his name is coming up here, and I don't know what this other name -- what this thing could be. As for Zeljko Zvilic, that's another name. At this time, he was working in Gracac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And are they both criminal police officers, are they, Zvilic and Petkovic?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were detectives. Zvilic was a detective. I don't know about Petkovic. I don't know if he was a uniformed policeman, whether he was a regular police or a crime police officer. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And you say Zvilic was a detective. Was he subordinate to you?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between me and him, there were other people in the chain of command. If he was an officer of the second station, then there was also the assistant for the crime police of the second police station. This is the Zadar police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And could I just clarify. You referred to two criminal police who worked at the reception centre. Yesterday, you mentioned three persons who worked there. Was it two, or was it three persons who worked at the reception centre in Knin?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. There were three police officers, but I can't recall these two names. I know that Zjelko Zvilic worked in Gracac. I don't why his name appears here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kardum --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as for the Petkovic person, I really can't recall. I don't know if he was assigned there or not. I said that I remember three names, Slavko Raspovic, Dejan Klanic, and Bozo Razov. Whether there was anyone else, I cannot confirm with any certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: When these three crime police were involved in a criminal investigation for a serious offence such as killing, were you informed of that investigation?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should have been informed, and I was aware of almost all investigations if we're speaking about investigations into murders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And at the time that the criminal police became involved, would they immediately inform you?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they informed me, and I had two men in my department who worked in the same field. They were inspectors for violent crime, sexual crimes and murders. One of them was Ivica Ducic. He had a university degree; and the other one was Krsmis Ivicevic [phoen]. He was a high school-level educated policeman, and these two men mainly investigated such criminal offences. The detectives would only assist them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I intend to refer to a document that has been admitted into evidence under seal, and I wonder if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Margetts, you may proceed where you addressed the issue by mistake to some extent also in private session, the issue of the material and the way in which you'd like to present that to the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. There are two issues that are the subject of some disagreement between the parties. The first issue is raised by the Cermak Defence, which relates to the absence of the crime registers from the 65 ter exhibit list of the Prosecution. The second issue is an issue raised by the Gotovina Defence in relation to the table that the Prosecution has produced. If I may first address the issue of the source documents - that's the crime registers - and the history of our acquisition of those and our submission now to have them added to the 65 ter exhibit list, the history is that the crime registers were received in two batches in late December, on the 20th of December and then the 31st of December. They were processed in the ordinary way. They consist of approximately 270 pages of information, and they have been submitted for translation. The translation of these materials has only been completed in August of this year, and similarly the cross-referencing of these materials to other materials we have and the production of the table has been completed also relatively recently. The materials were disclosed, again, in two batches. Three of the crime registers were disclosed to the Defence in early June of this year, and four of the tables were -- or the registers were disclosed to the Defence in early July of this year. So that's the history of the disclosure of these materials and the current situation that they're not on the exhibit list. Of course, they were received many months after we filed the exhibit list, and the translation was complete a number of months after we filed our last application to add documents to the exhibit list, and that calls for the necessity of this oral application today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you why it took so much time between receiving these documents and to disclose them to the Defence? It seems that there's the 20th of December you mentioned and then 31st of December and then disclosure, so approximately half a year later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The disclosure of these documents followed the analysis of the materials rather than preceding it and was in conjunction with the analysis of the materials I could -- I may better say because our final analysis followed the translation of the materials. So it was -- they were not immediately disclosed for the reason that the Prosecution itself did not grasp the entire relevance and -- of the materials upon their receipt but did have a better grasp of the materials at a later time. And just in relation to the materials and their relevance to this -- the issues that arise in this proceeding, one of the main reasons I have asked that the -- the witness remove his earphones is the fact that throughout the course of this examination there has been multiple references to these registers as part of the procedure for the reporting of crimes and the record of crimes in these registers being one of the first steps in initiating any investigation into crimes. Necessarily, a lot of the information that's contained in these registers is duplicated in complaints that go to the prosecutor's office, and in some sense the information in these registers underlies the information and to some extent repeats the substantive information that we find in Exhibit D511 and that we find in D568. So our submission is that these crime registers are relevant, as one of the -- the first steps in determining whether or not any specific crime would be investigated; and, secondly, that these crime registers are effectively source material that underlies the previous submissions of D511 and D568. So we say there's nothing novel in these registers. There's nothing novel in terms of the issues that these registers address; and in fact, we did an analysis and 360 of the entries that appear in these registers in fact appear in D511, and another number, I think 48, just off the top of my head, or a number in and around 48, of the entries that appear in these crime registers appear in source material obtained by the Gotovina Defence, and that material was utilized in the production of the previous exhibits D511 and D568. So at this stage we say these are probative. They are the source material, and they are not -- they don't present novel information. There's nothing in them that -- that at this stage is dramatically new to the parties. Furthermore, in terms of their presentation -- in terms -- so we say they will be a very useful addition to the exhibit list and very useful to the Trial Chamber in their consideration of the nature of the activities of investigation of crimes. As regards this witness, quite clearly he has indicated already that he would be able to look at these registers and provide useful information in relation to their source and their method of compilation and the use that they were put to, and it's for that reason that we bring this application, and it's for that reason that we do so with this witness present. Similarly, and if I could move on to the table of crimes that we've produced, we -- again, I'll reemphasise the submission I made in short form when we -- before we moved out of private session. And that is that this effectively -- the table effective presents the information in the crime registers in a form which is digestible and we hope useable by the Trial Chamber. So as for the submission in relation to the crime registers, we say there's nothing new or novel in this table. It just assists both the parties and the Trial Chamber in handling this information and using this information, and again, it would be useful for this witness to be given the opportunity to comment on the table that we've produced and the information that that table conveys. Your Honour, that concludes my submissions. If there are any particular questions you may have ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would first give an opportunity to the Defence to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We object to the admission to the 65 ter list of both the chart created by the Prosecution and the other underlying registers for now. As I had indicated to Mr. Margetts, the issue for us at this moment is not relevance or probative value because we haven't been -- we haven't had a fair opportunity to even look at the documents. As the Chamber is aware, throughout the course of these proceedings the Prosecution has from time to time added or asked or filed a motion to add additional documents to the 65 ter list. I think all three Defences have been very reasonable in consenting to the admission of those documents. Typically because the documents are one or two pages, maybe a few more, we have a reasonable opportunity to review the documents and to prepare for cross-examination of the witness. The specific problems here for the Defence are, for example, the compilation by the Prosecution, which purports to be somewhat of a summary of the underlying documents, is itself approximately 100 pages long. That should indicate to the Trial Chamber, if the summary is 100 pages, how much underlying material we have to go through in order to assess -- assess the reliability of, A, what the Prosecution has put together; and, B, to see if in the underlying materials there may be evidence that we would put to the witness in cross-examination to counter whatever inferences the Prosecution will try to make either with the underlying documents or the exhibit that they have prepared. I would note that in the Exhibit D568 which was the Defence exhibit, it took the Prosecution roughly two months to put together on paper their specific objections to review all the materials that we had submitted. It took them two months to go through that and then to file something with the Trial Chamber identifying specifically what they object to. We here received the chart I believe on Thursday night - it may be Wednesday night, but it's Wednesday or Thursday of last week - for the first time. That had never been disclosed to us before. With respect to the issue of the disclosure to the Defence of the underlying documents in June, I believe at status conferences or at 65 ter conferences the Gotovina Defence alerted the chamber and the Prosecution to the problem of disclosure under Rule 66(B) and Rule 68, which I believe is the case here. We do get rolling disclosures from the Prosecution but not a notice that says we received these documents and we will be filing a motion pursuant to Rule 65 ter because we intend ultimately to use this exhibit at trial. For us, there's a big difference in how we prepare or how much time we spend reviewing a thousand pages if the Prosecution tells us, for example, this could be exculpatory material that we're disclosing to you under Rule 68 or it's 66(B), which is sort of a broad category that does not indicate that the Prosecution intends to use this material at trial. In addition to the question Your Honour posed about why if the documents were received in December they only were disclosed in June, we have the additional question, which is: If the documents were sent for translation in June, why not give us notice that -- here's the disclosure; by the way we've asked for translations, and we intend do file a motion to amend the 65 ter exhibit list to add them. In addition with this witness in his 92 ter submission, there is a request to expand the Rule 65 ter exhibit list, which I believe there was no objection to in terms of the requests that are in writing with the 92 ter motion. Now we have several hundred if not thousands of pages to go through on an oral motion even after the written 92 ter submission asking for quite voluminous material to be added and put to this witness. Now, what I indicated to Mr. Margetts was, all we are asking is for we need a fair opportunity to review the materials; and at this point, Your Honour, I can say to you that if they are allowed to put this to the witness, we are not in a position to cross-examine this witness on this material. I did say to Mr. Margetts that after we'd had a few weeks to go through the material and see if there's an objection, we may agree with him that there's probative value in these documents, that they're relevant to this case, and that they should be admitted to the Rule 65 ter list and admitted before the Chamber. The problem is when we receive something on a Wednesday or a Thursday night before a Monday witness involving this volume of material, we simply cannot reasonably be expected to be able to cross-examine a witness on it, particularly where the Prosecution has now alerted the Chamber that they want to put -- that they are moving to amend the 65 ter list because they need to put matters to this witness, which from our perspective only further emphasises the fact that if, in fact, this is material that they need to put to this witness, it will likely mean that it's material that we would want to cross-examine the witness on, and we're not in a position to do it at this point. So for that reason, Your Honour, our position is that it not be put to this witness at this time because the Defence not able to cross-examine on it and that we be given a reasonable amount of time - I would ask for a couple of weeks - to go through the material, see if we have any objection to it, and then see if we can't put this material to another -- a witness. There are additional witnesses that are -- that will be, I believe, competent to address these matters. I won't be more specific than that in open session, but future witnesses that might be able to address the underlying documents, and there we may have more of a fair opportunity to put questions to future witnesses about these issues. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Nothing to add, Your Honour. It's a question of adequate notice for the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have nothing to add to my learned friend's submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We apparently have two issues. The one is the way in which this document was compiled. I wonder whether it would be of -- whether it would be useful at all to put questions to a witness on how you put together this information rather than perhaps put questions to the witness in relation to the underlying material. So may I take it that this is a matter of giving easy access to the Chamber to the material which we find in several source documents, and that, therefore, there's no need to put questions to the witness to that and that we could take -- leave to say that the Defence could take its time to see. Because if it's just compiling information which is already in other source material, then it primarily is a verification of whether things are put on the right lines and whether the links which are apparently created here are relevant or irrelevant links. That seems to be the first or - as a matter of fact, rather - the second issue. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I would agree with you, Your Honour, and again, let me say that our position is simply as it relates to putting questions to the witness about the materials. If the Prosecution wanted to proceed as we did with D568, which is to MFI it, give us an opportunity to go through it, and get back to the Chamber on what our position is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then we are talking about the tables --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- not about the material on which this table relies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Correct. And my second suggestion to Mr. Margetts was that if in fact much of this material is simply repeating what's already in D511 and D568, then if there are questions that need to be put to the witness, I would suggest that we put the D exhibits to the witness if in fact there is no difference or no substantive difference between the D exhibits and what the Prosecution has put together. But my issue is with putting the questions to the witness and not having an opportunity ourselves, then, in cross-examination to do the same with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I do understand that all of the information contained in this put-together document must be somewhere else and that the underlying material that questions could be put to the witness in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, even the underlying material hasn't been disclosed to us of the intents to use it with this witness so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There, of course, is an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And it's not on the 65 ter list. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but part of it is not on the 65 ter list, I do understand, and other of the material covered by this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: As I understand -- I could be wrong, and Mr. Margetts will correct me if I'm wrong. As I understood it, it was the exhibits that they are now asking to put on the 65 ter list, the underlying documents plus the exhibit or the document that the Gotovina Defence sent to them as the source material for D568. But even that document, the underlying document that we produced to them is also not on the 65 ter list as I understand it. So I'm not aware of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The -- one of the -- a substantial list that is very similar to the underlying document that the Defence have submitted to us is on the 65 ter list being a very extensive summary of Prosecution's presented by the Ministry of Justice of Croatia to the Prosecution, and that is on the list. So a lot of the material that's reflected in this table is also reflected in that document. Mr. President, I just had two small observations and possibly a practical proposal, and that is -- a very small observation is that the table, albeit it in small font, is not over 100 pages. It's 38 pages. The second observation I have to make is that the process for D568 and our review of it and why it took two months, it's a very different situation here because it was the lack of information in D568 that caused us to have to look to other sources and caused us to take time. So we still maintain our submission that the document is not too extensive and that because of its comprehensiveness, clarity -- and clarity, it is possible to -- for the Defence to grab hold of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's not talk about 38 or 100 pages because one picture comes to my mind. You know that sometimes Bibles are produced in a size of one centimetre by one centimetre. Whether that says anything about the information you would have to digest if you read is -- let's not -- it's perfectly clear, 38 or 100 pages, that my eyes might suffer under it in any way. Yes. Then -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I do have a practical suggestion. The real issue is a substantive and full cross-examination. The parties differ as to whether that's possible. The Defence submit that it's not. If it were possible for this witness to see the source crime registers and at least authenticate those materials, albeit that we'd have to go into the substance of those materials, that would be a helpful step in this process. Given his position, he seems the best witness to do that. And so we'd suggest that step at a minimum. We accept Your Honours' observations in relation to the table in effect that the table is the work product of the Prosecution. We consider it very helpful in focussing the witness and also providing substantial information to the witness that he could respond to, and we do think it may be helpful -- well, it would be helpful for him to be examined on it, but we also accept that it -- it is not essential that this witness be examined on that table. So our practical way forward, our suggestion may be that we present the underlying source documents to the witness. We have him review them. He's already made substantial comments about their relevance and their particular use in the crime investigation system, and potentially once the Defence have had the time that they've requested to review the material, it could be that it may be useful for the witness to be called back to address these materials and for him to be examined in relation to the -- these materials at a later time. So I'll just leave that option open as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Margetts. My recollection is not very clear. D568, which is a document which has some resemblance of what we see in front of us now, I tried to find out when it was admitted into evidence and when it was disclosed to the Prosecution for the first time. Could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I believe it was admitted through Witness 86, correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: There are two exhibits that I have referred to, Mr. President. One's D511, and D511 was presented during the course of the cross-examination of Witness 86.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah. That was on, as we find in your submission, the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And we accepted the good faith representations made to us by the Defence in relation to the source of that material, albeit secondary sources. We had no objection once we were able to discuss it over the break with the Defence, and we immediately consented to its admission because we could understand its utility for the Trial Chamber, plus the very practical way forward that the Defence had advanced by presenting that table. In regard to D568, the issue is a very different one. Again, we accept the representation as to source, and we're happy for its --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That put very specific question in relation to D568. Mr. Margetts, you are -- well, I noticed that sometimes people in answering a question go a bit broader than what is really asked to them. Then, therefore, the two-month included the summer recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it did, and I think there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: -- some communication between us about that. But just so we're clear, in specific response to your question, D511 came in through Witness 86. D568 is a bar table submission by the Defence in response to an issue that had arisen, I believe, with Witness 86, which would have been filed off the top of my head sometime in early to mid-July, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber considers that there's no need to immediately decide on the admission of the -- of the put-together document, the 37 pages. Therefore, the Defence will have time to consider what objections there are, if there will be any. Mr. Margetts, the Chamber will allow you to put questions to the witness in relation to the underlying source material to the extent it is not on your 65 ter list and to the extent it has not been announced as exhibits to be used in relation to this witness. The Chamber will very carefully listen to the type of questions that are put, the information that we receive in the answers, and we'll then either proprio motu or on an application by the Defence teams consider whether additional time should be given to prepare for further cross-examination on matters which we could not deal with at such short notice. That is how the Chamber would like you to proceed, and perhaps it's wise if you receive any other additional material soon to disclose it. If it's irrelevant, then the Defence might complain about being -- being loaded with irrelevant material. At the same time, we now get criticism that you have not provided to them in due time material that finally appears to be relevant. I am afraid that we'll never finally resolve this dilemma, but that's for the future. You may proceed as I indicated, and please keep in mind what the limits are, that by putting certain questions you might even create more complicated procedural problems as there are already now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Madam Registrar, if you could please present on the screen 65 ter 5288. Mr. President, we did have with us a binder with the -- the Croatian versions of the registers. It may be helpful if I provide that binder to the witness. I'll just check. Yes, Madam Usher. And, Mr. President, I've just presented a binder to Mr. Kardum that contains the crime registers that are listed sequentially on the exhibit list from numbers 37 to 43. That's 65 ter 5288 through to 5294.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you have before you crime registers from the police stations of Gracac, Obrovac, Benkovac, Drnis, Knin, Donji Lapac and Korenica. I'd first like to refer you to the first crime register in your binder, and if you could please have a look at that crime register, and you could confirm that that is the crime register for the Gracac police station containing the entries from August 1995 to December 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we see on the screen also what the witness is looking at because at this moment it seems to be correspondence rather than a register which appears on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, if we could move forward to past -- it would be about the third or fourth page. Okay. That's the first page of the register itself. The documents prior to that, the correspondence that I referred to in my submissions indicating the receipt of that from the officials of the Croatian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, have you had opportunity to go -- just look at the entries in that register and confirm that that is the fact the register for the Gracac police station?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only assume that this is the crime register from the police station of Gracac because I have never seen this crime register. I can only see by the last names that it could be that. I do not have the original in order to be able to confirm that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: But it is your -- it is consistent. Its layout and the information contained in it, is that consistent with your understanding as to how crime registers were compiled in the period August 1995 to December 1995 in the police stations under your command?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. If you could now move to the second tab in the binder --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just not confuse some things, please. Police stations were under the commander of the chief of the -- or commander of the police station. A police station is an organisational unit of the Ministry of the Interior, whereas the department of the crime police is not an organisational unit. It is just a form. So we had police stations, we had police administrations, and the ministry; three levels, in other words. I'm just a department as a part of the police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kardum, and you're absolutely right to correct me there. I did misspeak. Of course, the police station was not under your command. I was indicating that this would have been compiled by members of the crime department who were subordinate to you and, that's -- that is correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. But it -- this was so for a short period, but in the middle of September police stations started functioning just as all police stations in the Republic of Croatia. They had their normal organisational form: The commander of the police station, his assistant inter alia, also for the crime police, and then specific workers within the crime police organisation, because initially in this area the police stations did not have their own crime police. That was not envisaged in the organisational scheme. They were to have the crime police but not under the command of that police station, in other words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the question was focussing primarily on the format we see on the screen as the format of records kept; and where Mr. Margetts misspoke, I don't think that there's any basic misunderstanding in this respect, that you confirmed that this is how information was recorded within the police structure. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
