utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So if we could move to the next tab. And Madam Registrar, this is 65 ter 5290.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And this time, Mr. Kardum, the first page before you is 0624-4440, and then the next page along with the actual entries --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If, Madam Registrar, we could move to the next page on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- has an 8-digit marking, 0624-4441. And can you confirm, Mr. Kardum, that that document you're looking at is consistent with the crime register maintained by the police station of Benkovac in the period August 1995 to December 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it in that order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, could you come a bit closer to the microphone. The interpreters have some difficulties in hearing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said I don't have it arranged in that order. You said it was Drnis and then Benkovac. It is the same thing as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: So do you have before you the page on the left-hand side there marked 0624-4441, an 8-digit number stamped on it? Well, the 8-digit number on the page you're now looking at is that 0624-4440. Could you go back to the cover page.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Where is that? At the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you read that 8-digit number out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And this document that you have, a part of which or, in fact, the first page of entries is 0 -- is marked 0624-4441, is that consistent with the crime register that was maintained by the police station in Benkovac for the period August 1995 to December 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, could you please move to the next tab in your binder?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Margetts, I noticed that at least in the Obrovac document that "lagenda" appears on the bottom of the page, which is not a translation of what appears in the original but apparently is some kind of an assistance for non-native-speaking persons to understand what the entries mean. I put this on the record so if there's any issue with that, that I'd like to hear from the Defence. If the abbreviations or the explanations are not accurate, that the Chamber would be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And normally if, in the translation, anything appears which is not just a translation, Mr. Margetts, the Chamber would like to be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, and we will endeavour to complete that legend as well. I note that there are some entries where the expansion is unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, could you please refer to the next tab and to the document behind that tab. Now, just move past that correspondence, if you may, and if you could read out the -- that page there. Stop there. Move back. That page there in your hand there. Could you read out the 8-digit reference number on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar, if could you please present 65 ter 5292 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, can you please confirm that the document you have before you is consistent with the crime register for the Knin police that was maintained in the period August 1995 to December 1995.

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very fine print in the paper that I have so that I can hardly read a word of it, but according to its form I suppose that it could be that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. Now, if could you now turn back the pages in the binder and you could find the tab that is marked Drnis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Maybe if Madam Usher could assist the witness in moving through the binder. Thank you. And, Madam Registrar, if we could please have 65 ter 5291 presented on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, do you have before you a page which is marked with an 8-digit stamp, 0624-7886. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And is this document you have before you consistent with the crime register maintained by the Drnis police station in the period August 1995 to December 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station in Drnis was not a part of the Zadar-Knin police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate whether or not the document you have before you is consistent with a crime register maintained by the Drnis police station?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in the police station of Drnis. I never worked in it. It was never a component part of the police administration in which I worked. I can assume that it is consistent with it, but it's just an assumption on my part. That is as if you were asking me a question about the police station in Slavonia or in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Then I'll ask you this: Is the form of the document in front of you and the nature of the information entered in the document in front of you consistent with a crime register?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the crime registers were identical at the level of the entire state, I believe, so there is no reason for the one in Drnis to be different from the one in Knin or Zagreb or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Mr. Kardum, if could you now move with the assistance of Madam Usher -- and I apologise, Madam Usher; there are two to go - to the tab marked Donji Lapac? And again, Mr. Kardum, could you look at the first page there. Is the -- and could you read out the number that's stamped on that page?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, the same question again. Is this consistent, this document you have before you, consistent with the crime register maintained in Donji Lapac during the period August to December 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is. Just as I said in respect of the other ones, I can also say the same in respect of this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, if we could please present 65 ter 5293 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kardum, the final one -- and, Madam Registrar, if you please move to the next page of the B/C/S on ... yes, okay. Thank you. Now, Mr. Kardum, if you could please now move to the final tab, and that is the tab for Korenica. And again, if could you read out the 8-digit number on the final page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And Madam Registrar, if you could please present 65 ter 5294 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kardum, are you referring to the last page of the Korenica documentation?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Could you move through and refer to the first page in that tab. I apologise. I meant we'd move to the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kardum. And Mr. Kardum, is that consistent with the crime register maintained for the Korenica police station in the period August 1995 to December 1995?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it is because I can see the signature at the end, and that it was certified by the commander, Mr. Ivica --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last name you mentioned, the commander Mr. Ivica ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ivica Ugarkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's on the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kardum. That concludes my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And thank you very much, Mr. President. That concludes my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I see the binder that was shown to the witness. Mr. Margetts, for Drnis, where do I -- under what binder do I find Drnis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the tabs are marked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just ... Yes, we see, for example, in the Drnis, we ... Let me just try to understand what you are actually presenting, Mr. Margetts. The first page in the translation starts with lagenda, number, date of entry. I do not find any of these in the original first page that was just produced to the witness, do I? Apparently, that's 0624-7886.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the first -- I find something to the left at the top, 20-06-95. And then in the next column -- or are these the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It seems to me and I think that the issue is this, that up at the right-hand corner of the first page of the translation there's a reference to it being a partial translation. And it seems that it actually commences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- at page 0624-7897. And the explanation would be this, that the translations are ongoing, and the entries that have been selected and represented here are the ones relevant to this proceeding, and at this stage the translation is not complete in respect of all entries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you are referring and you are taking the witness to a page which may be there in the original but certainly is not there in translation, although the translation at the top says that it -- it refers to the same numbers, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yeah. It refers to the same range.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have nine pages there, we have in the original. We have many more, and now you say that we are -- it is presented to the Chamber -- a selection is presented to the Chamber, and I'm just trying to find out where -- that's the first page, the first --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- entry is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the -- that's Entry 105, date of entry, the 10th of October. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 105, 10th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I find this curious, Your Honour, because it seems that from that date there is a continuing entry to each entry number indicating that in fact this is not a selection related to the nature of the offences but is merely a partial translation from a period. I expect that the earlier period would have also been translated, and that may be it has not been uploaded into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Margetts, I'm doing my utmost best to -- on my computer to find originals, copy, et cetera, et cetera. You just put to the witness, do you see that number, is it the same as everything; and then only by carefully looking at it we see that apparently something the witness looks at and which starts in June 1995, what you're presenting to the Chamber is a selection of this document translated starting somewhere in October. I don't know how you have handled the further use of this material and what happened after that, but would you strongly contradict me if I say chaos?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You would contradict me, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I wouldn't contradict you directly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not strongly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I'd indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let matters be clear. This could be returned to Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It seems to be that the uploaded translation is incomplete, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But finally, the Chamber will have to understand what it sees on the screen. The Chamber will have to understand what the witness confirms and what the witness does not confirm; and therefore, more precision would be required. You have got 20 minutes to think about it, but you have no further questions to the witness, but everyone has 20 minutes to think about precision. We'll do the same. We will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, from the fact that you are on your feet, I take it that you will be the first one to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Kardum, you'll first be examined by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic is Defence counsel for Mr. Markac. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kardum. As Your Honour Judge Orie told you, I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Markac in this -- in these proceedings. Now let me ask you at the outset, do you know personally Mr. Markac?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Defence counsel, I've never personally been introduced to Mr. Markac. I have only heard of him in the media. I also know that he was the assistant minister for the special police, but I've never had occasion to be introduced to him or to work with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back and think about the historical context of the events that are at issue here in these proceedings, and I would like to refer to you paragraph 4 of your 2004 statement. This is Exhibit P896. You said that at this time - in other words, immediately before the outbreak of hostilities - about 85 to 90 per cent of the population of Zadar was Croatian; and yet, the ethnic composition of the police administration was such that about 70 per cent of the police force was of Serbian ethnicity. Is that consistent with what you remember?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After the tensions began to escalate of multi-ethnic nature, many people of Serb nationality left the area, including the policemen?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police were the first to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Some of them transferred to Zadar. They were transferred there, but some of them also left without any permission, just on their own free will?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I assume that of those police officers who were of Serb ethnicity and who left the police administration of Zadar were trained police officers, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were trained police officers. Many of them had attended police academy or the cadet school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did this situation affect the work of the police in Zadar in view of the fact that at one point in time they were left with a large number of experienced police officers gone?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was difficult to conduct all the police duties, especially so because the war broke out. Now, the war did not break out immediately. In the -- before the war, there were many incidents. People were killed, and many police officers were attacked and killed, and some of them were of Serb nationality. Many of them survived only because they claimed that they were Serbs. Others accused Croats of these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Kardum, but we have a limited amount of time, so let us please focus on the matters at hand. Now, I would like to ask you: In the organisational sense, how did the -- what was the position of the office itself, the police force? How did they try and make up for the large number of people who were leaving?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult. We tried to bring in new people, but very often these were people with very little police experience. They would just attend brief police courses of a few months, and then they would be assigned the simpler jobs; whereas the people who had some experience were assigned to more complex duties after undergoing difficult training.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Mr. Kardum, I failed to mention at the beginning, but we should both try - both you and I - to make a brief pause between question and answer and answer and question to allow the interpreters to interpret what we are discussing here in the same language, to interpret it into a language that the Court can understand. So please make brief pauses after my question. We know that a large number of policemen - we've heard it here in this case - that a large number of policemen were engaged in the establishment of the Croatian army, which was just then being established; and this, too, probably had an effect on the regular manpower of the police in Zadar, the police force in Zadar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So now we can discuss the events that are under review here in these proceedings, the events in the second half of 1995. In this context that we've just mentioned earlier, how would you assess the manpower levels of the police force of the police -- the Zadar-Knin police administration, in terms of the number of men and also their specialities?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the military police Operation Storm, we were set up in such a way to cover the free territory of the Republic of Croatia in the area of the Zadar-Knin county. This included the town of Zadar and about -- and an area of about five or six kilometres around Zadar, or -- I apologise, I should actually say five -- six to ten kilometres from Zadar, covering that area. And we also covered the area of Biograd. In this period, we were preparing the police forces in Zadar for the duties on the border, filling the posts at the border posts --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you please allow me to guide you, and then we will be more focused. Now, in your opinion, did you have a sufficient number of police officers, and were they qualified enough to conduct these important assignments?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not, so that we had to bring in men from elsewhere; in other words, the level, the manpower levels were reached with men from Zagreb; Benkovac received some men from Rijeka; Gracac, also from Rijeka; Lapac received some men from Split and Zadar. So we in Zadar did not have sufficient manpower levels to actually do all the -- carry out all the duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You've just answered my last question. So this was the situation in the police and also the crime police during and after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On January 1, 1995, you became the chief of the crime police. At this time, the chief of the police administration was Mr. Cetina, and his deputy was Mr. Pavlovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: There were -- you had some 50 subordinates in your chain of command, of whom about 12 crime scene examiners, and I'm talking here about the months of August and September 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, you've already mentioned briefly the types of jobs that the crime police had to deal with. In addition to your regular duties that are in the purview of any regular police, which is the discovery of crime perpetrators, traces of crimes and so on, you also had to engage in conducting interviews with people who were brought to the collection centres, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This was a demanding exercise, wasn't it, in the first two weeks after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very demanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I was just told by my colleague, and I will put a question to you because I don't want to anticipate. Now, when you said that police stations were -- that the opening -- the new vacancies were filled by people who came from other areas, tell me, did they know the area that they were going to work on?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't. We -- even we didn't know the entire area. I have to explain something. The Knin area was always under Sibenik. The Lika was always under the Gospic police station. Only in 1993 - and this was done on paper, in fact - they established the police administration, the Zadar-Knin police administration, but it did not really follow the county lines.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. I don't know whether you're interested to know the whole historic explanation of why they had no knowledge of the terrain, or that it is for the time being sufficient to establish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So this was one additional difficulty that certainly reflected the day -to-day work of the police in this area, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We mentioned the various duties that the crime police had to conduct. This was rather sensitive work, and I'm referring here to the investigation of mass graves, which were left behind once the earlier authorities left the area. This was also a demanding job, wasn't it, for the crime police?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. At the very outset when Operation Storm began, among other things, we were assigned this task as a priority. One of the priorities was to find mass and individual graves were Croats were buried; the purpose of this would be to exhume their bodies. In some cases, many of these were already of several years, and a lot of work was done in this respect. Your Honour, I have to address you now. I could not resist but bring a document that I believe no side here or no party here possesses, which describes the brutality of the powers, the authorities there. If you allow me, I would like to hand you this document so that can you see how a high political figure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, if there's any information you consider to be relevant, you can give it to the parties. The parties will then look at that material. They'll consider to what extent it supports or does not support the case they are presenting in this court, and then if one of the parties considers it to be relevant, then it will be put before us, and then -- and the scope of the evidence we're supposed to hear here is entirely in the hands of the parties and the Chamber itself. And on what the basis of what you just told us I see no reason already to invite you at this moment to provide us with material, as you said, you could not resist to bring to our attention. So you may provide it to the parties if you want to during your next break, or Madam Usher will assist you in giving it to the parties. Please proceed, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we said -- we described all the duties that had to be performed by the crime police in the regular period, when I'm referring to the pre-war period, something which is not in normal times the regular duties of the police?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. These were our first experiences with POWs, with mass graves, our first experiences in prosecuting war crimes and similar offences, so that we often wondered, not knowing exactly the delineation between a war crime and other offences, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This is quite clear. Let us look at Document P494 together. This was a document which was introduced by the OTP. It was tendered into the file and is in fact a document which was issued on the 4th of August by the assistant minister of the interior, Mr. Josko Moric on the 4th of August. By this document -- this document in effect regulates, or rather, orders the establishment and organisation of a collection centre. You have already referred to that, so that we will go through the first part of this document very quickly. On page 2 it says that a commander of the collection centre should be appointed, and if I'm not wrong there was another person who was excluded, as it were, from your criminal police department so that you remained without another person.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not hear the witness cause he overlapped with counsel and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The interpreters could not translate what you said because there was an overlap with the words spoken by Mr. Mikulicic. Could you re-start your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. This was a key person at least as far as I was concerned. Adem Mehmedovic. He was the general crime department head.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Item 4 of this document, which can you see on the screen, it is further stated that every collection centre should take particular care and create conditions in keeping with the Geneva Conventions and the obligations stemming therefrom, enumerating what they are - running water, maintenance of personal hygiene, sufficient number of lavatories, two meals a day, personal hygiene, toiletries, soap, and such - and, of course, to ensure the permanent attendance of medical and sanitary staff. My question is this: In your experience and according to the information that you have, were these requirements observed in the collection centre in Zadar, the way you perceive that today?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were absolutely observed. All the apprehended persons had hot water. There were some -- I can't say right off the cuff, but I believe seven or eight lavatories, or rather, bathrooms. Through the Ministry of Justice, I submitted this book, which I believe the OTP, has of the registered medical checkups of all persons and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These collection centre, or rather, this collection centre that we are specifically speaking about right now, the one in Zadar, was also visited by representatives of international organisations including the Red Cross, were they not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These representatives have unhindered contact with persons who were in the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. This was what we had to ensure for them according to the order. They were to speak in close quarters with each of the individuals who were there, and they availed themselves of this right. Of course, they did not talk to all the persons there, but selectively they did talk to a number of individuals, and we were not to be present at those interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, Mr. Kardum, did the Red Cross or any other international organisation raise any particular objections in respect of the conditions in the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no objections that were communicated to us. In fact, after these first contacts in the first talk that we had with them, they told us in brief that everything was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have already told us that members of the police, both in military police -- including the military police brought people to the collection centre and that a certain procedure was envisaged in terms of how to handle -- process every individual brought there, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We should go through that particular issue a bit later. But before that, I should like that ask the registry to bring up on the screen a document which is on the 65 ter list, which is 5277. This document which you will shortly see on your screen was sent on the 21st August, 1995, by the police administration of Zadar-Knin. We can see in the top right-hand corner Operative Action Return, and the date is indicated, it is sent to the Ministry of Interior to crime police department in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Margetts, that you want to add that it's not only on the 65 ter list, 5277, but it has been provisionally assigned P909?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We just recently received the list. So I'm not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I received it at the same time. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that when preparing your cross-examination you had not this list yet available. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'm grateful for your opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we said that this was a document which, in effect, constitutes a summary and that a description of events in the work of the collection centre in the sports hall Mocire in Zadar. I should like to draw your attention to -- to the conclusion in this document, which is on page 4 in the original version, and it states that as of the 4th of August, when the reception centre was established and open up to the 19th of August, when it was closed, it had been a centre for POWs in Zadar. And then it goes on to say that a total of 183 persons had been processed. That is stated on page 3 in paragraph 2, Item 3. With all these persons your people conducted interviews, did they not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your estimation in that period during the two weeks that transpired, how much time was actually spent for that particular exercise, for that particular job? Could you give us an estimate? And how many people were engaged on that?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were distributed in two shifts, approximately -- I can't say with precision, although I do have that list somewhere, but I think it was 20 people working per shift. The shifts worked for 12 hours, and then they would have free time for 12 hours and then again be on a shift. Very much time was spent on this. Some people were not ready to talk. Others lied. Yet others had to be taken to see the doctors. Yet others told the truth only after other people had told that they were -- had been somewhere at some particular place or time, and so these interviews sometimes had to be repeated. But at any rate, we had to finish the primary interview within 48 hours with the particular individuals and then transfer that person to the district attorney or release that person, or if they so wished, send them to the reception centre for civilians. But according to the law, we could not detain them for more than 48 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. So if during this brief interview, which was a summarized form of a crime processing of an individual, if it was established that there were reasonable grounds to believe that that individual had committed a criminal offence, a punishable criminal offence, then you would institute proceedings against such an individual, file a proper complaint, and so on and so forth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And this document further states or further contains the table of 183 registered persons who passed through the centre, and the action or the measure taken in respect of each individual is referred to. Let us save time, and we will not go through all that, but we can note that some were taken to Court; some others were released; others yet were taken to hospital, and so on and so forth. If we go on through this document, then we can see in conclusion that there are statistic figures given on page ERN 06105017 where it is stated that a total of 183 persons had been received, that 67 were released to a reception centres for civilians; a total brought before Courts were 115, and that six persons were transferred to other police administrations. According to what you remember, is this consistent with the actual situation?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I apologise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Be so kind as to look at another document, which is also on this list, the 65 ter list. The document is 5283.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My learned friend will help me with this document as well as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or am I making a mistake? No, I mentioned 5238, and it should be 83, which does not appear on the list, if I'm ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 5283.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is not on the list of documents attached to the 92 ter statement but perhaps is on the other list. I'll just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's number 46, and it hasn't been introduced previously. It's the investigations file.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, for Mr. Marko Bogunovic and it's not referred to that in the course of the examination-in-chief, so it hasn't received a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I will deal with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Mr. Kardum, what you see before you is a document. It is the Z-1 form. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the witness please be asked not to overlap with counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I again remind you not to start to answer the question when the interpreters have not yet an opportunity it translate the words of Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We have to bear that in mind, Mr. Kardum. The interpreters are having a hard time. So this is a document that would be filled in for each individual brought into the reception centre at which document was filled in by your people, was it not?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These documents were filled in by my people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So we can see here, we have the basic particulars of the person concerned. Now, to go to page 2, or rather, page 3 because page 2 is identical to the first one but without a photograph. Then we see a form Z-2. This form Z-2 is somewhat different. It has four model questions which your people were, I suppose, to ask of the interviewers -- interviewees?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The first question was whether the interviewees, the people who had been brought to the collection centre, whether they had any information about minefields or any other explosive barriers or obstacles; some had and others didn't. Wasn't that not the case?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this concrete example, Mr. Marko Bogunovic informed your people - I'm reading - that minefields were between Stankovci and Vukosici from Cista Mala, Polaca, to Benkovac exclusively on the hills. And further on in Item 2, that in the village of Lepora near the transformer station there is an house in which there is a depot. What would be done with this kind of information obtained by your people from people in the reception centre?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: We most often referred these -- this information to the special police, particularly when we knew that there were some larger quantities of weapons or equipment in depots or hordes of ammunition because our special police had lorries with which it could transport such means, and it had a specialised staff for explosive devices to handle such equipment. We would inform the ministry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- what is the relevance -- of course, if you find out and the witness already testified yesterday that the interviews were focussing on the existence of minefields, for example, of course you take appropriate measures to either find that material, use it, protect your population against it, but that's not what this case is about. The Chamber earlier had to establish that 30 to 40 per cent of your questions are repetitious. Mr. Mikulicic, could you please try to focus on new information the Chamber will receive rather than to go through the whole of the examination-in-chief without much adding to that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will do so, Your Honour, but my intention was to present that the police, so-called, fundamental police was not equipped for that kind of job. So they need to pass the information to some others units. But I will proceed, Your Honour. I will move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Item 21 of your 2004 statement, you said that with your people you managed to cover the area as far as that was possible. What I would like to know is, what was the procedure when, for instance, the police station or somebody individually came across a body, a dead body, or a place that one could assume was a place where a crime had been committed? What was the obligation of the fundamental, of the regular police in such a situation?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such information came most often to the police station because that is how they were laid out in the field, and the police station had -- police stations had regular police only after the 28th or the 29th of August or the beginning of September. It was only after that date that they had some criminal policemen as well. They were obliged to inform the operations duty service of the police station of any such incidents, and then the chief of that service would also be informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it -- obviously, we have some problems with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It seems that we missed part of the answer. Could you resume there where you said -- now we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now we have. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It apparently was a technical problem what appears on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Kardum. Now, tell us, did a regular police officer who was in the field, did he have a duty to provide security for the -- to block off the site of crime and to make sure that any traces of the crime were preserved. That seems pretty obvious, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was his primary duty. That was the primary duty of the regular police. Once they reached the site of a crime, they have to secure the crime and make sure that any -- that any traces be recovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is clear. However, what was the procedure if already at this first level one could observe that there were other unauthorised individuals who had been on-site and that the site itself had already been altered? What would the procedure be then?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, the person conducting the investigation, be it the investigating judge or a police inspector, in other words, a crime police officer, they would have to note that in the note, and they would have to describe the alterations to the crime scene and what type of alterations and how altered they were. I don't know if this is a proper reply to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: It is. Now, to the best of your recollection, in view of the fact that there were many members of various international organisations in the field, I mean here, the civilian police of the UN, the monitoring teams of the UN, and the European Community who often came to the sites where crimes had been committed, were there instances where they actually contaminated the crime scene? Was that possible, and what is your observation that?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was quite possible. As the chief of the crime police, I never, not in one instance did I receive any information about a crime having been committed by a member of an international organisation. I think our colleagues who were there could not really be -- take pride in the fact that they didn't inform the chief of the crime police because even they - and this would be only one person - would receive information from another source, especially in view of the fact that members of the international organisations and the domestic Serbs, people who were from our area, trusted those organisations, those members more than they did the local police. We have to bear in mind that this was the time following a 4-year war, and it was difficult for a person to suddenly begin placing his trust in the Croatian police as being the police that would protect them and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, your question was clearly about whether the crime scene was ever changed or contaminated, but now the answer had almost nothing to do with that. Why not ask the witness to answer your question, the question simply being whether although -- whether it was possible. I can tell you, Mr. Mikulicic, everything is almost possible, but apart from that detail, did you ever receive a report on a specific crime scene which was contaminated by members of an international organisation, having changed or contaminated the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that there were such cases, but I can't really recall. I can't give you a specific example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't exclude the possibility, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: My colleague just stressed my attention to the fact that we have some problems in translation, and this is concerns to the previous answer of the witness when I asked him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take that the suspicion of international --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- having committed crimes. That came as a bit as a surprise as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, if you could seek a clarification of that part of the answer, that would put record straight, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kardum, probably because we are speaking too fast, the interpreters are having difficulties. I asked you whether you received complaints or reports from members of international organisations on crimes committed. What was your reply?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received any complaint or report from any member of an international organisation on a crime having been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have meetings with members of international organisations to discuss how to improve the work of the police in discovery of perpetrators of criminal activities?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really recall, but I think we did have one such meeting. I think I had one such meeting, but I can't really recall how many persons were present. I think there were several members of several international organisations present, but I can't tell you exactly who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let's take an example. If a body was found in the field and if a member of the regular police came out to the field, how was the assessment made, whether this body was there as a result of a criminal offence or whether the death was of natural causes or perhaps collateral damage as a result of the combat activities; and who made this type of assessment?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't know who would make such an assessment, but I assume that special attention was always given to the way the body looked. If the body was decomposed, and this was on the 10th, 12th, or 14th of August that the body was found, then what would be noted was that the body was decomposed, and then this would be attributed to sanitation activities. But who actually made the assessment, whether this was done at a headquarters of the operations, operative action, I really couldn't tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, my question also has to do with the procedure that was in place. Now, if this dead body was of an individual who was -- who died either of natural causes or as a result of the combat activities, then the hygiene and sanitation measures would have been implemented by the civilian protection, right?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. They would conduct the sanitation of the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: However, Mr. Kardum, you told us that the team that would go on site in order to conduct the hygiene and sanitation measures also had in its ranks a crime scene investigator. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There would always be one crime scene examiner, and if you recall that communication from Mr. Maric, I think, of the 5th or 6th of August, it was sent from the Ministry of the Interior, it actually referred to prints being taken in order -- fingerprints in order for the identity of the body to be established. If that was not possible, then the identification would be impossible. The other thing that had to be done is that the body would have to be photographed. There would have to be two photographs made, and these photographs would have to be sent undeveloped to the Ministry of the Interior in Zagreb. I don't know what they did with the undeveloped film there, but we couldn't have done it on our premises because we didn't have the equipment for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if it was assessed that a body that was found on the ground was not of a person who was a victim of a crime, then the crime police would not have to take any steps, correct?

utterances.speaker: IVE KARDUM [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The crime police in those cases would not take any action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like us to take a look at a document. This is a document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I seek one clarification. Your testimony was that if -- well, let's say on the 12th of August, you would find a body which was already decomposed to some extent, that you would attribute it either natural death or combat activities. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We wouldn't attribute it to natural causes. We would only establish that the causes were natural if a pathologist was also on the scene of the crime. There were such cases where the pathologist, a forensic expert, would be there, and then that forensic expert would establish that there was no violence involved. This was done on Form KT-10 for each body, each individual. However, if the body was decomposed, then the civilian protection would collect that body before the photographing was done. They would place a metal plate next to the body with a number, and if the body was identified based on some identification mark or identifying mark, then the name of that person would also be included on the plate. If not, then we would just write unidentified, "NN." So what would be entered on these forms would be the first and last names of the person; the status of this individual, whether it was a civilian or a soldier, depending on what uniform that person had on at that time. There were some other items that had to be entered in the form, but in any case there would be the place where they were buried, the identification number, and the serial number. They did not necessarily correspond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Should I move on, Your Honour, or should I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just a bit puzzled by what we find as an answer on page 93, lines 21 and following. The KT-10 form would be filled in by whom? Would it be the forensic experts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The crime scene examiner. They would be the one to fill it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The crime scene examiner would always be present if the sanitation services would remove a body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So they would never remove a body unless a crime scene examiner was present and would fill in such a form?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, no. There -- an on-site investigation was not always conducted when the KT-10 form was filled out. The KT-10 form would have to be filled out in every single instance, but that does not mean that there was an on-site investigation conducted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not talking about an on-site investigation. I'm just talking about a sanitation team who would go to a place where a body was found which was to some extent was decomposed after a couple of days. What kind of report would be made, and by whom exactly? So the first question, whether in such circumstances there would always be a crime scene examiner accompanying the sanitation team that took care of the body.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they would always fill in such a form.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now do I understand that dependant on the assessment of the cause of death, it would then be decided whether another investigation, an on-site investigation was needed or what one would do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. You could say -- say that. That was one of the criteria on the basis of which the on-site investigation would be conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the -- those who were in charge of sanitation would then return to where they came from and leave the crime scene to an on-site investigation. Is that -- so they would not take the body; they would leave the body where it was, return to their own premises, and an on-site investigation would then be conducted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know if they would leave the scene. They would -- more often than not, they would wait for the other group to come. This would be in outlying areas. They would go there by car, so they wouldn't go back until a district attorney arrived, in the case where a police team would come and carry out -- conduct the on-site investigation. In these cases too, many of these incidents would be attributed to human sanitation, subjected to human sanitation. So --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the place where the witness -- that the witness mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said in these cases, too, many of these incidents would -- were attributed to human sanitation, subject to human sanitation, and then you added something the interpreters did not hear. Could you repeat that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In some cases where classic on-site investigations were conducted, full investigations where the pathologist would be there, the district attorney, the investigating judge, so everyone was in the field, in those cases, those victims, too, were subjected to human sanitation. Now when did this not happen? This did not happen when there were no family members present who could show where the person could be buried. In all other cases, these persons were also subjected to human sanitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I need a bit more explanation on what exactly "human sanitation" means in this context. That might not be fully clear to me. I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Mikulicic. We have to stop for the day. Mr. Kardum, we'll adjourn for the day, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon in this same courtroom. And I would like to instruct you as I did yesterday that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, whether already given or still to be given. We will adjourn and resume at the 24th of September, quarter past 2 in this same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 24th day of September, 2008, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
